Joe Cool's First Appearance
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/peanuts-1.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1

Snoopy has imagined himself as everything, but none of his alter egos are as effortlessly ridiculous as Joe Cool. The character first appeared in the May 27, 1971, Peanuts strip, when Snoopy suddenly decided he was a college student hanging around the student union. Linus even plays along by asking how he did in chemistry class, but Joe Cool has bigger concerns. He thinks chemistry is a drag, and being seen around campus is clearly much more important. That first strip is simple but already contains almost everything that makes Joe Cool work.

All Snoopy needs to turn into him are his sunglasses and an extremely laid-back attitude. Later strips expanded the joke by turning his doghouse into a dorm room and letting Joe spend more time around the student union while he chased the college experience without showing much interest in actually going to class. The official Peanuts description still calls him the “ultimate big beagle on campus,” which is about as accurate as it gets. More than anything, Joe Cool works because he exaggerates a side of Snoopy that was already there. The character has never suffered from a lack of confidence, but Joe Cool turns that into an entire personality.

Dark and Stormy Night - World's Shortest Novel
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/peanuts1-1.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Peanuts comic strip by Charles M. Schulz featuring Snoopy acting as an aspiring author on top of his doghouse

blocks.x: Image via Peanuts Worldwide

Snoopy may be a terrible novelist, but nobody can question his commitment to the craft. His writing career officially began in the July 12, 1965, Peanuts strip, when he dragged a typewriter onto the roof of his doghouse and began with the immortal words, “It was a dark and stormy night.” From there, Snoopy’s world-famous author persona became one of Schulz’s funniest recurring ideas, as the beagle spent years trying to write the great American novel from the least original opening imaginable.

The joke was even smarter than it first appeared. Of course, Snoopy did not invent the sentence. It comes from Edward Bulwer-Lytton’s 1830 novel Paul Clifford and had already become a famous example of overwrought writing by the time Schulz borrowed it. That was exactly the point, though, as Snoopy approached the cliché with complete seriousness. Schulz took the gag even further in 1971 with Snoopy and “It Was a Dark and Stormy Night,” a published book built around Snoopy’s adventures as an author. The actual novel may not be much, but as a Peanuts joke about ambition and confidence, the strip is still perfect.

https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/screenshot-2026-09-16-025334-1.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Peanuts comic strip by Charles M. Schulz showing the very first appearance of Snoopy

blocks.x: Image via Peanuts Worldwide

Any list like this would obviously be incomplete without Snoopy’s actual debut. It is almost strange to look back at Snoopy before he became the character he is today. He made his first Peanuts appearance on October 4, 1950, just two days after Schulz launched the strip. The character’s introduction doesn’t feature his iconic doghouse or any mention of his many personas. Instead, the strip shows Snoopy wandering beneath Patty’s window box and ending up soaked when she waters her flowers.

This simple moment turns the future star of Peanuts into the punchline of a hilarious visual gag. What’s fascinating is how early Snoopy actually behaved much more like an ordinary dog, while the huge personality and imagination that would eventually define him came much later. Nobody reading this tiny four-panel joke could have known that the nameless little dog would eventually become a novelist, fighter pilot, college heartthrob, and arguably the most recognizable character any comic strip has ever produced. The first Snoopy strip is not his funniest or most imaginative adventure, but as beginnings go, it feels extremely special in hindsight.

His writing career officially began in the July 12, 1965, Peanuts strip, when he dragged a typewriter onto the roof of his doghouse and began with the immortal words, “It was a dark and stormy night.” From there, Snoopy’s world-famous author persona became one of Schulz’s funniest recurring ideas, as the beagle spent years trying to write the great American novel from the least original opening imaginable.

The joke was even smarter than it first appeared. Of course, Snoopy did not invent the sentence. It comes from Edward Bulwer-Lytton’s 1830 novel Paul Clifford and had already become a famous example of overwrought writing by the time Schulz borrowed it. That was exactly the point, though, as Snoopy approached the cliché with complete seriousness. Schulz took the gag even further in 1971 with Snoopy and “It Was a Dark and Stormy Night,” a published book built around Snoopy’s adventures as an author. The actual novel may not be much, but as a Peanuts joke about ambition and confidence, the strip is still perfect.

Snoopy’s First Appearance

Image via Peanuts Worldwide

Any list like this would obviously be incomplete without Snoopy’s actual debut. It is almost strange to look back at Snoopy before he became the character he is today. He made his first Peanuts appearance on October 4, 1950, just two days after Schulz launched the strip. The character’s introduction doesn’t feature his iconic doghouse or any mention of his many personas. Instead, the strip shows Snoopy wandering beneath Patty’s window box and ending up soaked when she waters her flowers.

This simple moment turns the future star of Peanuts into the punchline of a hilarious visual gag. What’s fascinating is how early Snoopy actually behaved much more like an ordinary dog, while the huge personality and imagination that would eventually define him came much later. Nobody reading this tiny four-panel joke could have known that the nameless little dog would eventually become a novelist, fighter pilot, college heartthrob, and arguably the most recognizable character any comic strip has ever produced. The first Snoopy strip is not his funniest or most imaginative adventure, but as beginnings go, it feels extremely special in hindsight.
